claim: Targeted sequencing of sixteen SLE risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases and controls produced a comprehensive dataset of the variations causing susceptibility to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: Targeted sequencing of sixteen SLE risk loci among 1349 Caucasian cases and controls produced a comprehensive dataset of the variations causing susceptibility to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
evidence: The abstract states this as a direct result of the study's methodology and findings.

claim: Two independent disease association signals in the HLA-D region identified two regulatory regions containing 3562 polymorphisms that modified thirty-seven transcription factor binding sites.
source: Two independent disease association signals in the HLA-D region identified two regulatory regions containing 3562 polymorphisms that modified thirty-seven transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: The abstract presents specific quantitative findings from the HLA-D region analysis.

claim: Variations modifying the consensus binding motifs of IRF4 and CTCF in the XL9 regulatory complex modified the transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1 in a chromosome-specific manner.
source: Variations modifying the consensus binding motifs of IRF4 and CTCF in the XL9 regulatory complex modified the transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1 and HLA-DQB1 in a chromosome-specific manner
evidence: The abstract describes specific molecular mechanisms identified in the study.

claim: SLE risk genotypes result in a 2.5-fold increase in the surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ molecules on dendritic cells, which increases to over 4-fold after stimulation.
source: resulting in a 2.5-fold increase in the surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ molecules on dendritic cells with SLE risk genotypes, which increases to over 4-fold after stimulation.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative measurements of surface expression differences.

claim: Analyses of fifteen other SLE risk loci identified 1206 functional variants tightly linked with disease-associated SNPs.
source: Similar analyses of fifteen other SLE risk loci identified 1206 functional variants tightly linked with disease-associated SNPs
evidence: The abstract summarizes findings from additional loci analyzed in the study.

claim: Common disease alleles contain multiple causal variants modulating multiple immune system genes.
source: demonstrated that common disease alleles contain multiple causal variants modulating multiple immune system genes.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a general conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease resulting from a profound loss of immune tolerance to self-antigens.
source: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease resulting from a profound loss of immune tolerance to self-antigens (Olsen and Karp, 2014; Theofilopoulos, 1995a; 1995b; Fairhurst et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The disease initiates with the production of autoantibodies against a spectrum of self-antigens (typically >10 in SLE patients), focused on nucleic acids and nucleic-acid-associated proteins.
source: The disease initiates with the production of autoantibodies against a spectrum of self-antigens (typically >10 in SLE patients), focused on nucleic acids and nucleic-acid-associated proteins.
evidence: This describes established characteristics of SLE pathology.

claim: Disease pathology begins with the deposition of immune complexes in various target tissues, leading to the activation of inflammatory effector mechanisms that damage critical organ systems.
source: Disease pathology begins with the deposition of immune complexes in various target tissues, leading to the activation of inflammatory effector mechanisms that damage critical organ systems.
evidence: This describes the pathological mechanism of SLE based on established knowledge.

claim: Patients with SLE can present with combinations of symptoms, including skin rashes, oral ulcers, glomerulonephritis, neurologic disorders, severe vasculitis, and a distinct form of arthritis.
source: Patients with SLE can present with combinations of symptoms, including skin rashes, oral ulcers, glomerulonephritis, neurologic disorders, severe vasculitis, and a distinct form of arthritis (Tsokos, 2011).
evidence: This clinical description is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Susceptibility to SLE is caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
source: Susceptibility to SLE is caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors (Fairhurst et al., 2006; Harley et al., 2009; Deng and Tsao, 2010; Rai and Wakeland, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Genome-wide association analyses (GWAS) have identified more than 50 SLE risk loci to date.
source: Genome-wide association analyses (GWAS) have identified more than 50 SLE risk loci to date, indicating that susceptibility is quite polygenic (Harley et al., 2009; Nath et al., 2008; Harley et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2012; Graham et al., 2006; 2008; 2009; Hom et al., 2008; Gateva et al., 2009; Relle et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple GWAS citations.

claim: Targeted genomic sequencing of twenty-eight GWAS-confirmed SLE risk loci was performed using Illumina custom enrichment arrays on genomic DNA from 1775 SLE patients and controls.
source: Targeted genomic sequencing of twenty-eight GWAS-confirmed SLE risk loci was performed using Illumina (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) custom enrichment arrays on genomic DNA from 1775 SLE patients and controls (Supplementary file 1A, Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This describes the study methodology with reference to supplementary data and figures.

claim: The sequencing procedures resulted in >128 fold coverage of the genomic segments containing these SLE risk loci.
source: These procedures resulted in >128 fold coverage of the genomic segments containing these SLE risk loci (Supplementary file 1B, Figure 1G).
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of sequencing depth with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The bioinformatics pipeline defined 1349 samples of European American (EA) ancestry that carried 124,552 high quality variants of which 114,487 are single nucleotide variations (SNVs) and 10,065 are insertion/deletions (In/Del).
source: Our bioinformatics pipeline (Figure 1H) defined 1349 samples of European American (EA) ancestry (Figure 2A) that carried 124,552 high quality variants of which 114,487 are single nucleotide variations (SNVs) and 10,065 are insertion/deletions (In/Del).
evidence: This provides specific quantitative results from the bioinformatics analysis with figure references.

claim: The sequence-based variant database identifies an average of one variant every 39 basepairs in the targeted regions.
source: This sequence-based variant database, which identifies an average of one variant every 39 basepairs in the targeted regions, provides a comprehensive assessment of genomic diversity at SLE risk loci in the EA population.
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of variant density in the dataset.

claim: The sequence analyses identified 70,070 previously annotated variations and 54,482 novel or unannotated variations within the EA cohort.
source: Overall, these sequence analyses identified 70,070 previously annotated variations and 54,482 novel or unannotated variations within the EA cohort.
evidence: This provides specific counts of annotated versus novel variants.

claim: Functional annotation defined about 40% of the variants in the dataset as regulatory, based on their inclusion in eQTL datasets or their localization into ENCODE-defined regulatory segments.
source: Functional annotation defined about 40% of the variants in the dataset as regulatory, based on their inclusion in eQTL datasets or their localization into ENCODE-defined regulatory segments (Figures 2B,C).
evidence: This provides a quantitative assessment of functional variants with figure reference.

claim: Multiple variants in 26 of the 28 risk loci were strongly associated with susceptibility to SLE.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, multiple variants in 26 of the 28 risk loci were strongly associated with susceptibility to SLE
evidence: This summarizes association analysis results with figure reference.

claim: Seven loci reached genome-wide significance (p≤5 × 10-8), ten reached suggestive significance (p≤5 × 10-5), and nine reached confirmatory significance (p≤10-3).
source: with seven loci reaching genome-wide significance (p≤5 × 10-8), ten reaching suggestive significance (p≤5 × 10-5), and nine reaching confirmatory significance (p≤10-3) (tabulated in Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This provides specific statistical thresholds and counts of significant loci.

claim: The study replicated associations previously reported in SLE GWAS for 36 SNPs at ten loci.
source: We also replicated associations previously reported in SLE GWAS for 36 SNPs at ten loci (Supplementary file 1E)
evidence: This describes replication of known associations.

claim: 673 variants in the sequencing data set exhibited similar or stronger associations with disease than published tagging SNPs, and 345 of these were categorized as functional.
source: As tabulated in Supplementary file 1F, 673 variants in the sequencing data set exhibited similar or stronger associations with disease than published tagging SNPs, and 345 of these were categorized as functional.
evidence: This provides specific counts of variants with stronger associations than known SNPs.

claim: Multiple, new variants had the strongest disease-associations in 27 of the 28 risk loci and 14 of the peak variants are annotated as functional.
source: These results show that multiple, new variants had the strongest disease-associations in 27 of the 28 risk loci and that 14 of the peak variants are annotated as functional.
evidence: This summarizes findings about novel peak variants.

claim: Conditional analyses identified four risk loci with multiple, independent signals: NMNAT2-SMG7, TNFSF4, HLA-D, and XKR6.
source: As shown, conditional analyses identified four risk loci with multiple, independent signals. This indicates that NMNAT2-SMG7, TNFSF4, HLA-D, and XKR6 each contained two or more LD blocks with potentially regulatory variants which might be contributing to disease susceptibility independently.
evidence: This describes results from conditional analysis identifying independent signals.

claim: 1206 functionally annotated variants were in tight LD (D'>0.8) with the 21 peak risk signals and all but 7 of these were non-coding, regulatory variants.
source: As shown, 1206 functionally annotated variants were in tight LD (D'>0.8) with the 21 peak risk signals and all but 7 of these were non-coding, regulatory variants.
evidence: This provides specific counts of functional variants in LD with peak signals.

claim: Multiple functional variations are in tight LD with the peak disease associated signal in every risk locus.
source: These results demonstrate that multiple functional variations are in tight LD with the peak disease associated signal in every risk locus.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Sequence analysis of the HLA-D region revealed 15129 common variants (1 variant/29.6 bp) distributed throughout the 448 Kb segment analyzed.
source: Sequence analysis of the HLA-D region revealed 15129 common variants (1 variant/29.6 bp) distributed throughout the 448 Kb segment analyzed.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative data about variant density in HLA-D.

claim: More common (15129) than rare (12076) variants were detected in HLA-D, which differs significantly from the roughly 5-fold excess of rare variants that are typically detected throughout the human genome.
source: More common (15129) than rare (12076) variants were detected in HLA-D, which differs significantly from the roughly 5-fold excess of rare variants that are typically detected throughout the human genome and at other SLE risk loci in our study (Abecasis et al., 2010; 2012; Hu et al., 2014) (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This compares HLA-D variant frequencies to genome-wide patterns with citations.

claim: The preponderance of common variants in the HLA-D sequence dataset is consistent with an ancient origin of these HLA-D polymorphisms within the human lineage.
source: The preponderance of common variants in this sequence dataset is consistent with an ancient origin of these HLA-D polymorphisms within the human lineage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variant frequency data.

claim: 3786 variations in HLA-D are nominally associated with SLE (p<0.05) and 1797 of these have annotated regulatory functions.
source: As shown, 3786 variations in HLA-D are nominally associated with SLE (p<0.05) and 1797 of these have annotated regulatory functions.
evidence: This provides specific counts of SLE-associated variants in HLA-D.

claim: Five separate segments within HLA-D contained variants achieving genome-wide significance for association with SLE.
source: Five separate segments within HLA-D contained variants achieving genome-wide significance for association with SLE.
evidence: This summarizes the number of significant association signals in HLA-D.

claim: The peak SLE association was with rs9271593 (p=6.50E-10), which is one of 687 SLE-associated regulatory variants mapping to the XL9 regulatory component.
source: The peak SLE association was with rs9271593 (p=6.50E-10), which is one of 687 SLE-associated regulatory variants mapping to the XL9 regulatory component within the intergenic region separating DRB1 and DQA1 (Majumder et al., 2006; Majumder et al., 2008).
evidence: This identifies the peak association variant with statistical support and citations.

claim: The XL9 segment of HLA-D is not adequately covered by SNP typing arrays such as the Immunochip v.1, possibly accounting for the failure to detect this potent SLE association in previous GWAS analyses.
source: As shown in Figure 5Aiii & iv the XL9 segment of HLA-D is not adequately covered by SNP typing arrays such as the Immunochip v.1, possibly accounting for the failure to detect this potent SLE association in previous GWAS analyses.
evidence: This is an inference about why XL9 was not detected in previous studies, supported by figure data.

claim: Conditional analyses identified three independent disease associations in HLA-D, each localized to important regulatory or coding elements.
source: Thus, these conditional analyses identified three independent disease associations, each localized to important regulatory or coding elements within HLA-D.
evidence: This summarizes the results of conditional analysis in HLA-D.

claim: More than 150 variations within the HLA-DRB1 through HLA-DQB1 segment are eQTLs that have been shown to impact the transcription of 72 genes in various immune cell lineages.
source: As shown in the top tract within Figure 6A, more than 150 variations within this small genomic segment are eQTLs that have been shown to impact the transcription of 72 genes in various immune cell lineages (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This provides specific counts of eQTL variants and affected genes with figure reference.

claim: All of the MDM eQTL variants impacting HLA-DR and DQ expression are associated with variants in XL9.
source: All of the MDM eQTL variants impacting HLA-DR and DQ expression are associated with variants in XL9 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the association between eQTL variants and XL9 with figure reference.

claim: XL9 contains binding sites for multiple factors affecting chromatin structure (CTCF, ZNF143) and has been shown to assemble HLA-DR and HLA–DQ proximal promoters into a transcriptional complex.
source: XL9 contains binding sites for multiple factors affecting chromatin structure (CTCF, ZNF143) and has been shown to assemble HLA-DR and HLA–DQ proximal promoters into a transcriptional complex that facilitates coordinate, tissue-specific transcription (Bailey et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2008; Whitfield et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the functional role of XL9 supported by multiple citations.

claim: IRF4 up-regulation of MHC class II molecules was shown to be strongly associated with disease severity in a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: Notably, IRF4 up-regulation of MHC class II molecules was shown by these investigators to be strongly associated with disease severity in a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
evidence: This cites findings from another study about IRF4 and disease severity.

claim: Thirteen of the fifty-six potent regulatory variants in the XL9 haplotypes are located within a 1 Kb segment in the center of XL9.
source: Thirteen of the fifty-six potent regulatory variants in the XL9 haplotypes are located within this small segment.
evidence: This provides specific counts of regulatory variants in a defined region.

claim: Five of the XL9 variants are located in the consensus binding sites for CTCF, ZNF143, or IRF4 and are predicted to impact their binding properties.
source: Five of these variants are located in the consensus binding sites for CTCF, ZNF143, or IRF4 and are predicted to impact their binding properties (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes predicted functional effects of specific variants with figure reference.

claim: For both IRF4 variants, alleles carrying the unmodified IRF4 consensus binding sequence are associated with the risk haplotypes, while those with nucleotides that are less common to the consensus motif are present in all of the non-risk haplotypes.
source: For both of these variants, alleles carrying the unmodified IRF4 consensus binding sequence are associated with the risk haplotypes, while those with nucleotides that are less common to the consensus motif are present in all of the non-risk haplotypes (Figure 5F, Figure 6C, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the association between IRF4 motif variants and risk haplotypes with figure references.

claim: The HAP2 and HAP3 alleles of variants within the XL9 segment are strongly associated with increased transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 in MDM cell cultures.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, the HAP2 and HAP3 alleles of variants within this short segment, including an IRF4 motif variant, are strongly associated with increased transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 in our eQTL panel of MDM cell cultures and in datasets from the literature (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes eQTL associations with figure reference.

claim: Coding region variants linked with XL9 risk associated regulatory variants are present in a significantly higher proportion of RNA-SEQ reads than coding variants linked to protective alleles.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, coding region variants linked with XL9 risk associated regulatory variants are present in a significantly higher proportion of RNA-SEQ reads than coding variants linked to protective alleles.
evidence: This describes allele-specific expression data with figure reference.

claim: XL9 regulatory variations modulate the level of transcription of HLA-DR and HLA-DQ in a chromosome-specific manner.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that XL9 regulatory variations modulate the level of transcription of HLA-DR and HLA-DQ in a chromosome-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the allele-specific expression experiments.

claim: HLA-DR surface expression is roughly 2.5-fold higher on unstimulated MDDC from a HAP3 (risk) homozygote in comparison to a HAP1 (protective) homozygote.
source: As shown in Figure 7A.1 and A.2, HLA-DR surface expression is roughly 2.5-fold higher on unstimulated MDDC from a HAP3 (risk) homozygote in comparison to a HAP1 (protective) homozygote.
evidence: This provides quantitative flow cytometry data with figure reference.

claim: The increased surface expression of HLA-DQ is maintained on dendritic cells following activation with the TLR7/8 ligand R848 over 18 hours.
source: This increased surface expression of HLA-DQ is maintained on dendritic cells following activation with the TLR7/8 ligand R848 in a time course over 18 hours, indicating that HLA-D risk haplotypes drive higher levels of HLA class II molecule surface expression during TLR activation and dendritic cell maturation (Figure 7C.3–C.8).
evidence: This describes time-course expression data with figure reference.

claim: The transcription of several genes within the HLA complex are strongly upregulated in lymphoblastoid cell lines from risk versus protective XL9 haplotype homozygotes in the 1000 genome RNA-SEQ data set.
source: Finally, the transcription of several genes within the HLA complex are strongly upregulated in lymphoblastoid cell lines from risk versus protective XL9 haplotype homozygotes in the 1000 genome RNA-SEQ lymphoblastoid cell line (Lappalainen et al., 2013) data set (Figure 7D).
evidence: This describes analysis of public RNA-seq data with citation and figure reference.

claim: HAP3 of the XL9 signal is strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (OR 2.0, p<7.04 E-08).
source: This identified 56 functional variants that formed 12 haplotypes of which HAP3 was strongly associated with SLE susceptibility (OR 2.0, p<7.04 E-08)
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for a haplotype.

claim: HAP1 (OR 0.58, p<1.63 E -06) and HAP6 (OR 0.34, p<1.69 E-07) of the XL9 signal were protective.
source: while HAP1 (OR 0.58, p<1.63 E -06) and HAP6 (OR 0.34, p<1.69 E-07) were protective (Figure 5D,E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for protective haplotypes with figure reference.

claim: The protective and risk haplotypes in XL9 form separate clades at opposite ends of the MJ network.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, MJ analysis found that the protective (shaded in blue) and risk (shaded in red) haplotypes form separate clades at opposite ends of the network, indicating that these two extremes in disease association are also extremes in the divergence of regulatory variations.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic relationship of haplotypes with figure reference.

claim: HAP4 of the DQB1 5' segment signal was protective (OR 0.3, p<3.88 E-09) and HAP2 condoned risk (OR 1.9, p<1.11 E-06).
source: The twenty eight variants formed seven haplotypes of which HAP4 was protective (OR 0.3, p<3.88 E-09) and HAP2 condoned risk (OR 1.9, p<1.11 E-06).
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for DQB1 5' segment haplotypes.

claim: HAP6 of the DRB1 signal is protective (OR 0.4, p=4.58E-05) and HAP1 is risk (OR 1.6, p=1.50E-06).
source: As shown in Figure 8Biv, they form 8 haplotypes of which HAP6 is protective (OR 0.4, p=4.58E-05) and HAP1 is risk (OR 1.6, p=1.50E-06).
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for DRB1 signal haplotypes with figure reference.

claim: Composite HLA-D haplotypes formed eleven haplotypes that accounted for more than 90% of all of the chromosomes identified within the EA panel.
source: The composite analysis formed eleven haplotypes that accounted for more than 90% of all of the chromosomes identified within the EA panel (Figure 8D).
evidence: This provides a quantitative measure of haplotype coverage with figure reference.

claim: HAP1 (p=2.38E-07, OR = 0.59) and HAP6 (p=1.01E-06, OR = 0.42) of the composite HLA-D haplotypes are protective.
source: As shown, HAP1 (p=2.38E-07, OR = 0.59) and HAP6 (p=1.01E-06, OR = 0.42) are protective
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for protective composite haplotypes.

claim: HAP3 (p=4.56E-09, OR = 2.1), HAP2 (p=0.032, OR = 1.3), and HAP11 (p=0.0172, OR = 2.3) of the composite HLA-D haplotypes are risk.
evidence: This provides specific association statistics for risk composite haplotypes.

claim: Chromosomes carrying risk-associated variants show consistent and highly significant increases in transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 in MDM cultures from eleven heterozygotes.
source: As shown in Figure 8E, an assessment of chromosome-specific transcription in MDM cultures from eleven heterozygotes for the rs9271593 (peak XL9 signal) revealed consistent and highly significant increases in transcription of HLA-DRB1, HLA-DQA1, and HLA-DQB1 for chromosomes carrying risk-associated variants.
evidence: This describes allele-specific transcription data with figure reference.

claim: HLA-DRB1_0301 and HLA-DQB1_0201 were the most strongly associated HLA-D class II alleles in the EA cohort.
source: As shown, HLA-DRB1_0301 and HLA-DQB1_0201 were the most strongly associated HLA-D class II alleles in this analysis, which is consistent with several previous studies of HLA-D associations with SLE (Morris et al., 2012; Armstrong et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2011; Furukawa et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2014; Fernando et al., 2012).
evidence: This identifies the most strongly associated classical HLA alleles with citations to previous studies.

claim: XL9 regulatory polymorphisms can completely remove the associations of HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQA1 imputation variants with SLE.
source: The top plot illustrates that XL9 regulatory polymorphisms can completely remove the associations of HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQA1 imputation variants with SLE, but does not remove the DQB1 imputation or 5' region regulatory haplotype associations.
evidence: This describes results from conditional analysis.

claim: Variations in XL9 and HLA-DRB1 class II alleles are in tight LD and represent a combined contribution to SLE.
source: These analyses indicate that variations in XL9 and HLA-DRB1 class II alleles are in tight LD and represent a combined contribution to SLE, while variations in the segment 5' of DQB1 independently contribute to SLE susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from conditional analysis results.

claim: All homozygotes for regulatory HAP3 (peak risk) are also homozygous for DRB1_0301, DQA1_0501, DQB1_0201, which is the HLA-D class II haplotype found in the extended DR3 haplotype.
source: Notably, all homozygotes for regulatory HAP3 (peak risk) are also homozygous for DRB1_0301, DQA1_0501, DQB1_0201, which is the HLA-D class II haplotype found in the extended DR3 haplotype (Kachru, 1984; Smolen et al., 1987; Hohler and Buschenfelde, 1994; Schur et al., 1990; Niu et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the association between regulatory and classical HLA haplotypes with citations.

claim: The DR and DQ alleles that have been associated with SLE in previous studies of EA cohorts are found among the regulatory risk haplotypes and are absent from the protective clade.
source: Overall, the DR and DQ alleles that have been associated with SLE in previous studies of EA cohorts are found among the regulatory risk haplotypes and are absent from the protective clade (Morris et al., 2012; 2014; Niu et al., 2015; Ramos et al., 2010).
evidence: This summarizes the relationship between classical HLA alleles and regulatory haplotypes with citations.

claim: Maximal risk for disease is associated with specific haplotypes typically composed of five or more functional variations that are in strong LD with the peak risk variant.
source: First, maximal risk for disease is associated with specific haplotypes typically composed of five or more functional variations that are in strong LD with the peak risk variant.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from analysis of multiple risk loci.

claim: The overwhelming majority of functional variants in SLE risk loci are in regulatory elements (1199 of 1206).
source: The overwhelming majority of these variants are in regulatory elements (1199 of 1206, Table 1) and carry ENCODE scores indicating that they are potent functional polymorphisms.
evidence: This provides a quantitative summary of functional variant types.

claim: The risk and protective/non-risk haplotypes are typically at opposite ends of the MJ networks (15 of 16 risk loci).
source: MJ analysis revealed that the risk and protective/non-risk haplotypes are typically at opposite ends of the networks (15 of 16 risk loci), indicating that significant variations in disease risk are most strongly associated with multiple functional changes.
evidence: This summarizes a pattern observed across multiple loci.

claim: Peak risk haplotypes have greater odds ratios for SLE susceptibility than individual peak tagging SNPs from the original published GWAS studies.
source: As tabulated in Table 2, peak risk haplotypes have greater odds ratios for SLE susceptibility than individual peak tagging SNPs from the original published GWAS studies and from the targeted association studies performed here.
evidence: This compares haplotype and SNP odds ratios.

claim: The peak risk haplotype had a higher odds ratio than the peak GWAS tagging SNP for 13 of 16 loci, resulting in an overall 17% increase in the average odds ratio.
source: Overall, the peak risk haplotype had a higher odds ratio than the peak GWAS tagging SNP for 13 of 16 loci, resulting in an overall 17% increase in the average odds ratio for the sixteen loci tested.
evidence: This provides a quantitative summary of odds ratio improvements.

claim: The cumulative risk associated with the GWAS tagging SNPs for all sixteen loci sums to 6.04 fold, while the same value for all peak risk haplotypes is 8.8.
source: As tabulated in Table 2, the cumulative risk associated with the GWAS tagging SNPs for all sixteen loci sums to 6.04 fold, while the same value for all peak risk haplotypes is 8.8
evidence: This provides cumulative risk calculations.

claim: The peak risk haplotypes at sixteen risk loci account for 66% of the population attributable risk for SLE within the EA cohort.
source: As shown in Figure 14B and tabulated in Supplementary file 3B, the peak risk haplotypes at these sixteen risk loci account for 66% of the population attributable risk for SLE within this EA cohort (Supplementary file 3A and 3B).
evidence: This provides a PAR calculation with figure and supplementary file references.

claim: The five SLE risk haplotypes (HLA-D, STAT4, IRF5, ITGAM, and UBE2L3) are present at variable frequencies within all of the European, South American, and South Asian populations.
source: As shown in Figure 14C, these five risk haplotypes are present at variable frequencies within all of the European, South American, and South Asian populations.
evidence: This describes the global distribution of risk haplotypes with figure reference.

claim: The five SLE risk haplotypes are much less frequent in the African populations sampled and, with the exception of UBE2L3, absent from the East Asian populations.
source: However, they are much less frequent in the African populations sampled and, with the exception of UBE2L3, absent from the East Asian populations.
evidence: This describes population-specific frequencies of risk haplotypes.

claim: These five SLE risk haplotypes likely arose prior to human global colonization and were present with divergent frequencies in the ancestral founding populations of modern ethnic groups.
source: Based on this distribution, it is likely that these haplotypes arose prior to human global colonization and that they were present with divergent frequencies in the ancestral founding populations of modern ethnic groups.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary history of risk haplotypes based on their distribution.

claim: Individuals homozygous for XL9 HAP3 (risk) variations have more than two-fold higher surface expression for HLA-DR and DQ molecules at baseline which increases to 4-fold after stimulation with TLR-ligand on monocyte-derived dendritic cells than HAP1 (protective) homozygotes.
source: Our data demonstrate that individuals homozygous for XL9 HAP3 (risk) variations have more than two-fold higher surface expression for HLA-DR and DQ molecules at baseline which increases to 4-fold after stimulation with TLR-ligand on monocyte-derived dendritic cells than HAP1 (protective) homozygotes (Figure 7).
evidence: This provides quantitative expression data with figure reference.

claim: The XL9-mediated increase in surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ in dendritic cells is predominantly responsible for the association of XL9 regulatory haplotypes with susceptibility to SLE.
source: Based on these data, we hypothesize that the XL9-mediated increase in surface expression of HLA-DR and DQ in dendritic cells is predominantly responsible for the association of XL9 regulatory haplotypes with susceptibility to SLE.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression data.

claim: A total of 1651 functional variants are present in XL9 and 1912 functional variants in the DQB1 5' segment.
source: Overall, we identified a total of 1651 functional variants in XL9 and 1912 functional variants in the DQB1 5' segment
evidence: This provides specific counts of functional variants in two regulatory regions.

claim: Twenty-three transcription factor binding sites in XL9 and fourteen in the DQB1 5' segment are strongly modified by the extensive variations present within these genomic segments.
source: As tabulated in Figure 15A.ii, twenty-three transcription factor binding sites in XL9 and fourteen in the DQB1 5' segment are strongly modified by the extensive variations present within these genomic segments.
evidence: This provides counts of affected transcription factor binding sites with figure reference.

claim: The regulatory characteristics of the XL9 and DQB1 5' transcriptional complexes will be highly diversified among HLA-D haplotypes.
source: Overall, we identified a total of 1651 functional variants in XL9 and 1912 functional variants in the DQB1 5' segment, indicating that the regulatory characteristics of these transcriptional complexes will be highly diversified among HLA-D haplotypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high number of functional variants.

claim: Both the protective and risk HLA-D haplotypes are present with varying frequencies throughout the global population.
source: Interestingly, as shown in Figure 15B, both the protective and risk haplotypes that we identified for the entire HLA-D region are present with varying frequencies throughout the global population.
evidence: This describes the global distribution of HLA-D haplotypes with figure reference.

claim: These regulatory HLA-D haplotypes have evolved together with the HLA class II coding regions over long periods.
source: These findings are consistent with the characteristics of other highly polymorphic regions of HLA, including the HLA-D class II coding alleles, and indicate that these regulatory haplotypes have evolved together with the HLA class II coding regions over long periods.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary history based on haplotype characteristics.

claim: These regulatory variations represent an essential and highly selected characteristic of the diversification of HLA-D that strongly impacts a variety of immune functions.
source: Given all of these characteristics, we propose that these regulatory variations represent an essential and highly selected characteristic of the diversification of HLA-D that strongly impacts a variety of immune functions.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the cumulative evidence about regulatory variation.

claim: An analysis of available eQTL databases identified a total of 72 genes whose transcription levels are reported to be modulated by variations in the HLA-D region.
source: An analysis of the available eQTL databases identified a total of 72 genes whose transcription levels are reported to be modulated by variations in the HLA-D region.
evidence: This summarizes findings from eQTL database analysis.

claim: Essentially all of the HLA class II molecules and a variety of gene products involved in antigen processing, peptide loading, and surface expression are up-regulated by the HAP3 risk haplotype.
source: As shown, essentially all of the HLA class II molecules and a variety of gene products involved in antigen processing, peptide loading, and surface expression are up-regulated by the HAP3 risk haplotype.
evidence: This describes expression patterns associated with the risk haplotype.

claim: Regulatory polymorphisms in HLA-D affect a plethora of immune system genes that are involved in various pathways of the adaptive immune system.
source: However, these results indicate that regulatory polymorphisms in HLA-D affect a plethora of immune system genes that are involved in various pathways of the adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the eQTL analysis.

claim: The Illumina custom enrichment system theoretically captured sequence information for ~99.94% of the ~4.4 Mbs of genome targeted in these risk loci.
source: The Illumina custom enrichment system theoretically captured sequence information for ~99.94% of the ~4.4 Mbs of genome targeted in these risk loci.
evidence: This describes the technical efficiency of the sequencing approach.

claim: Target enrichment was highly specific and efficient, typically resulting in >70% of reads on target and resulting in >128X average coverage for the 28 risk loci analyzed.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1A, target enrichment was highly specific and efficient, typically resulting in >70% of reads on target and resulting in >128X average coverage for the 28 risk loci analyzed (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This provides quantitative measures of sequencing quality with figure reference.

claim: Continuous sequences could be derived for >85% of the targeted intervals in assembled sequences.
source: In general, continuous sequences could be derived for >85% of the targeted intervals in assembled sequences, with only extended regions (i.e. >1 Kb) of highly repetitive sequences failing to assemble.
evidence: This describes the completeness of sequence assembly.

claim: The concordance of sequence-based SNV calls versus SNV calls with the Illumina Immunochip was >99.8% for samples with >25X average coverage.
source: In addition, the concordance of sequence-based SNV calls versus SNV calls with the Illumina Immunochip was >99.8% for samples with >25X average coverage (Figure 1G), which supports the overall accuracy of variant detection throughout the genomic segments assayed.
evidence: This provides a validation measure of variant calling accuracy with figure reference.
